key_concept: Law of Dominance: when true-breeding plants with contrasting traits are crossed, the F1 is heterozygous ($Tt$) and expresses only the dominant trait.
steps: Mendel crossed true-breeding tall ($TT$) and true-breeding dwarf ($tt$) pea plants. The gametes are $T$ and $t$, so every F1 plant is $Tt$.
Assertion A: all F1 plants were tall and none were dwarf. This matches Mendel's monohybrid cross observation, so A is correct.
Reason R: stem height was one of Mendel's seven pairs of contrasting traits, with tall dominant over dwarf. R is correct.

Linking R to A: in $Tt$ plants the dominant allele $T$ masks the recessive allele $t$, so every F1 plant shows the tall phenotype. Dominance of tall over dwarf therefore directly explains why the F1 contains no dwarfs.
Both statements are true, and R correctly explains A, so option (1) is the answer.
final_answer: Option (1): Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
why_not_others: Option (2) would require dominance to be unrelated to the uniform tall F1, but dominance is exactly what causes it. Options (3) and (4) fail because both statements are factually correct.
common_trap: Students mix up F1 with F2 and expect a $3:1$ tall-to-dwarf ratio. That ratio appears only in F2, after the $Tt \times Tt$ self-cross.
time_saving_tip: Ask whether R answers 'why A?'. Here 'Why is the F1 all tall?' is answered by 'Because tall is dominant', so pick option (1) directly.
